newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FOCUS - Rebels, landslide disrupt Colombian oil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rebels, landslide disrupt Colombian oil.

text.p: Back-to-back dynamite attacks by Marxist rebels and a huge landslide have halted production in Colombia's northeast Cano Limon oil field for the second time in less than a month.

The pipeline which pumps crude to the Caribbean coast port of Covenas is ruptured in three different places and will take until at least Friday to fix, a spokesman for the state-run oil company Ecopetrol said Monday.

The situation prompted Occidental Petroleum Corp, the main operator at Cano Limon, to declare force majeure in the field, which effectively allows it to temporarily suspend all contracts with contractors and its own employees.
"Given the events we are going ahead and declaring force majeure in our Cano Limon field," an Occidental spokesman told Reuters.

Ecopetrol, which is in charge of operating the Cano Limon- Covenas pipeline declared force majeure on the transport of crude -- a legal mechanism that permits it to suspend pumping for lengthy periods without penalty.
But so far neither Ecopetrol nor Occidental have decided on whether to declare force majeure on loadings and exports of Cano Limon crude, most of which is destined for U.S. Gulf Coast refineries.

There is limited storage on-site at Cano Limon equivalent to about three days production 175,000 bpd. Occidental tends to scale back production until on-site storage tanks are full and then it shuts in production.

The Ecopetrol spokesman said. "We set force majeure on the transport of crude because of the serious nature of the damage that will not be repaired until at least Friday, but we have not taken any decision on exports. We're still evaluating what our lifting schedules are and how much crude we have in storage at Covenas."

National Liberation Army (ELN) rebels blew up the pipeline over the weekend in two separate attacks, one 41 miles (67 km) the other 218 miles (350 km) west of Cano Limon. The landslide broke the pipeline and destroyed a nearby road 79 miles (127 km) west of the field.

The Ecopetrol spokesman said a so-far undetermined amount of crude spilled into the River Nuevo Presidente, close to the border with Venezuela adding that measures had been taken to contain the slick.
The attacks occurred before Ecopetrol engineers had managed to repair the pipeline in the wake of a separate blast last Wednesday, which resulted in the spillage of 6,000 barrels of crude.

The latest bombings demonstrate the growing ease with which the ELN is able to paralyze oil production even though about one- third of the army's active fighting force of about 100,000 men is deployed in protecting oil infrastructure.

The Cuban-inspired rebel army, set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966, has blown up the pipeline, the second largest in the country, 45 times this year -- the same number of time as in the whole of last year.
More than 140,000 barrels of crude have been spilled this year compared with 105,000 barrels in 1996.

In addition the rebels have adopted the tactic of blasting the pipeline several times in the space of just a few days, which is proving more effective in paralyzing production than the isolated attacks of the past.
When Occidental declared force majeure on production on July 15 it was the first time since the field came into operation more than 10 years ago.

The new declaration of force majeure, the second in just three weeks, is bound to raise new questions about the Colombian security forces' ability to safeguard key oil infrastructure and will disrupt Occidental's plans to produce an average 171,000 barrels of crude per day from Cano Limon throughout 1997.
